title: A shared home. A little less guesswork.
intro: A ten-minute house conversation, a worked split and a simple weekly reset.
alt: Housemates sharing the Saturday morning kitchen routine
paragraphs: The useful first question is not who owes what. It is what you have agreed to share. Put rent and utilities in one list, optional things such as groceries and subscriptions in another, and leave personal purchases out.

Choose the people and the split before a bill arrives. Equal shares are a starting point, not a rule. If someone moves in halfway through the month or uses something differently, agree an exact amount or percentage together.

sections.title: A £60 shop, worked through
paragraphs: Four housemates agree to share a £60 food shop equally. Alex pays at the till. Each person’s share is £15. Alex has covered their own £15, and Jordan, Taylor and Casey each owe Alex £15.
If Jordan has already transferred £15, record that repayment and let Alex confirm receipt. Do not add the repayment as another shopping expense: that would count the same cost twice.

sections.title: Agree these five things
bullets: Which costs are shared, and who is included in each one?
Which split will you use for rent, bills and food? They do not have to match.
Who adds a bill, and when should everyone pay?
How will you handle a new housemate, a guest or time away?
When will you review the arrangement? Pick a date, not ‘later’.

sections.title: Make the rota specific
paragraphs: ‘Keep the kitchen tidy’ is hard to share. ‘Empty the kitchen bin by Thursday evening; Jordan this week, Taylor next’ gives a job an owner and a next turn. Agree how swaps work before a busy week arrives.

sections.title: The five-minute weekly reset
bullets: Add any missing shared costs and check the people included.
Confirm payments you have actually received.
Check next week’s jobs and agree any swaps.
Put one useful detail, such as bin day, somewhere everyone can find it.

title: Good work starts on the same page.
intro: Separate the cost of the space from the cost of the project, with a clear example for both.
alt: Two makers tidying their shared workshop
paragraphs: A studio has two kinds of shared spending: keeping the space running and making a particular piece of work. Mixing them makes it easy for somebody to pay for a project they are not part of.

Agree a short description, the people involved and the split before someone buys materials. Keep receipts alongside your usual business records. A shared-expense record is not a substitute for accounting or tax advice.

sections.title: One studio, two different splits
paragraphs: Three makers share £900 monthly studio rent equally: £300 each. Alex and Jordan then agree to share a £120 batch of clay for their own project. That expense includes only those two people, at £60 each. Taylor owes nothing for the clay.
If Alex paid both bills, Jordan owes Alex £360 and Taylor owes Alex £300. Alex’s own combined share is £360. Check: £360 + £360 + £300 = £1,020, the total spent.

sections.title: Before the next purchase
bullets: Name the project or shared running cost.
Agree the budget and who can approve extra spending.
Include only the people who agreed to share it.
Choose equal, exact, percentage or share-based amounts.
Record who paid, the total and the repayment date you agreed.

sections.title: Give the shared jobs an owner
paragraphs: Pair each recurring job with a name and a next turn. For example: ‘Restock packaging on Monday: Alex; next week: Jordan.’ Keep equipment instructions and space details separate from spending so people can find both quickly.

sections.title: Close the week cleanly
bullets: Review new costs while everyone remembers the context.
Record repayments made outside Commune and confirm money received.
Correct mistakes with a clear reason rather than quietly changing the story.
Keep the original receipts for your business records.

title: A little planning for a better trip.
intro: A shared booking, an optional activity and a clean finish, without turning the holiday into bookkeeping.
alt: Friends looking across the bay from a ferry
paragraphs: Before anyone books, agree what the group is sharing, a comfortable budget and what is optional. A person can be part of the trip without joining every meal or activity.

Keep the cost and who paid it in the same record. Add a booking while you still remember who is included. Discuss cancellation and changes using the provider’s actual terms, not an assumption that everyone will cover everything.

sections.title: The cottage and the kayak trip
paragraphs: Four friends share a £480 cottage equally, so each owes £120. Alex pays the booking. Later, only Jordan and Taylor join a £90 kayaking trip, paid by Jordan. That activity is £45 each for Jordan and Taylor; Alex and Casey owe nothing for it.

Keep the two expenses separate. Jordan, Taylor and Casey each owe Alex £120 for the cottage. Taylor also owes Jordan £45 for kayaking. Agree repayments from the actual records rather than assuming every expense belongs to all four people.

sections.title: Before you go
bullets: Agree a budget for accommodation and transport.
List optional activities separately and ask who wants in.
Check booking, refund and cancellation terms before paying.
Decide how to record costs in another currency; do not mix currencies as if they were the same amount.
Choose a date for the final check after you return.

sections.title: While you are away
paragraphs: Add the meal, taxi or booking once, with only the people who shared it. If someone pays for a friend’s portion, record what actually happened and agree how that friend will repay them. Do a quick check, then put the phone away.

sections.title: Finish with a clear record
bullets: Check the last receipts and any refunds together.
Resolve disputed costs before marking them paid.
Pay through the method you normally use outside Commune.
Record the payment and have the recipient confirm receipt.
